CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up for chronic problems, fatigue, and lightheadedness.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 58-year-old male with a past medical history of congestive heart failure and hypertension who presents for follow-up of his chronic conditions. He reports feeling out of sorts, tired, fatigued, and lightheaded every once in a while for about 5 weeks, starting around Labor Day. He states kitchen construction began over Labor Day weekend, making cooking difficult and causing him to eat out frequently. He reports occasional bloating, shortness of breath with exertion during home projects, slight chest cramps that resolve after about an hour, and a slight cough. He denies fever or chills.

Constitutional: Positive for fatigue and lack of energy. Negative for fever and chills.
Cardiovascular: Positive for lightheadedness and slight chest cramps.
Respiratory: Positive for shortness of breath with exertion and a slight cough.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Congestive heart failure.
Hypertension.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Currently completing home renovation and kitchen construction projects. Eats meals out frequently due to construction. Monitors blood pressure regularly at home with assistance from his wife.

MEDICATIONS
Lasix.
Lisinopril 20 mg daily.

3. Provider will follow up with the patient after test results are received.

Hypertension

She has been anemic since she was 13 years old. She did have heavy periods until she had a hysterectomy in 1996, but her doctors have not told her why they think she is anemic. She reports feeling not great, experiencing frequent fatigue during the day, feeling feverish with chills at times, shortness of breath and wheezing when trying to be active, headaches, chilling sensations, and getting cold so easily that she feels she has to really bundle up. She also reports that her anxiety and depression feel like they have been getting worse lately. She recently started taking her iron pills again after not taking them in about a year.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for fatigue, feverish with chills at times, chilling sensations, getting cold easily.
Respiratory: Positive for shortness of breath and wheezing when trying to be active.
Neurological: Positive for headaches.
Psychiatric: Positive for anxiety and depression feeling worse lately.
Negative for sleep apnea or use of oxygen at night.

SURGICAL HISTORY
Hysterectomy in 1996.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Drinks alcohol once or twice a year.

MEDICATIONS
Ferrous sulfate 25 milligram tablets, twice daily (one in the morning and one in the evening).
Vitamin B12 (over-the-counter).

PHYSICAL Exam
General physical exam template used. Heart and lungs auscultated. Abdomen examined with no tenderness where pressed. Physical exam is normal without any significant findings. No pacemaker or defibrillator.

ASSESSMENT
Long-standing iron deficiency anemia.

- Schedule an upper endoscopy (EGD) and colonoscopy to assess for potential sources of anemia or GI bleed. If these tests are inconclusive, a capsule endoscopy will be considered.
- Send a referral to Dr. Flores, hematologist, for evaluation regarding intravenous iron or assistance with iron storage.

- Schedule appointment for the referral to Dr. Flores.
- Follow instructions for the bowel prep.
- Take iron pills with orange juice for the next 8-12 weeks.
- Call the office with any questions or worsening symptoms.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Headaches and newly diagnosed pituitary lesion.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
52-year-old male with a newly diagnosed pituitary lesion seen in consultation at the request of Dr. Henry Howard for possible surgical intervention. Mr. Ward presented to his primary care provider, Dr. Howard, on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over the past few months. He denied any trouble with headaches in the past. Headaches are located behind his eyes, described as a dull nagging ache. Onset was about 3 months ago and they have been getting worse over time. Initial severity was 3 out of 10 and has gradually worsened to 6 out of 10 severity. Headaches tend to be worse in the morning, last a few hours at a time, and nothing makes them better or worse. He tried Tylenol a few times for the headaches but it did not work, so he stopped. He denies feeling sick, fever, rash, neck issues, numbness, tingling, or passing out. Recently, he has noticed he seems to be bumping into door frames. He does not think he has any change in vision or balance; his eyes were checked in the fall.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies feeling sick, fever. 
Skin: Denies rash.
Neurological: Complains of worsening headaches behind the eyes, dull nagging ache, severity 6/10, worse in the morning. Denies neck issues, numbness, tingling, passing out. Notes bumping into door frames recently. Denies changes in balance.
All other systems reviewed and are negative.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Unremarkable. Does not take any medicines.

SURGICAL HISTORY
None noted in the transcript.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Works as a computer programmer. Married for 25 years and recently bought a small house. Does not drink alcohol, smoke, or use recreational drugs, and never has.

FAMILY HISTORY
Patient was adopted, so family history is unknown.

MEDICATIONS
None.

ALLERGIES
None noted in the transcript.

RESULTS
Labs dated 3/3/21 personally reviewed: CBC, unes, coagulation, and CRP were all normal. Pituitary hormone profile demonstrates a low TSH; all other results were normal. 
Radiology studies: MRI for the brain with contrast from 3/4/21 personally reviewed. Reveals a pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles are normal in size and no other abnormalities are noted.

PHYSICAL EXAM
General: Alert, oriented to time, place, and person. Affect is appropriate and speech is fluent.
Cranial Nerves: Cranial nerve examination is grossly intact.
Motor/Sensory: No focal, motor, or sensory deficit in the upper or lower extremities.
Eyes: Visual acuity and eye movements are normal. Pupils are equal and reactive. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Color vision is normal.

ASSESSMENT
Pituitary adenoma. Mr. Ward is a very pleasant 52-year-old male who has a benign appearing pituitary adenoma, incidentally discovered during workup for worsening headaches. He is symptomatic with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression, therefore surgical intervention to excise and decompress the pituitary fossa is indicated.

PLAN
- Surgical intervention for excision and decompression of the pituitary fossa using a transsphenoidal approach (minimally invasive, going through the sphenoid sinus). Risks of anesthesia (heart attack, stroke, death) and surgery (infection, need for further surgery, wound issues such as spinal fluid leak or infection requiring prolonged hospitalization or additional procedure, seizure, stroke, permanent numbness, weakness, difficulty speaking, death) were discussed.
- Send removed adenoma to pathology to confirm diagnosis (appears to be a benign pituitary adenoma).
- Referral to an eye doctor for a full exam and a visual field test to map peripheral/side vision prior to surgery and monitor after surgery to see if vision is improving (may occur after surgery if not seen before).
- See surgery scheduler, Deborah, on the way out to get surgery scheduled fairly quickly and set up the pre-surgery visual field test.

INSTRUCTIONS
Call the office if you think of any questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Chest pain

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Betty Hill is a new patient referred by the ER for esophagitis. She experienced an episode of central chest pain located right behind her breastbone in early October 2020. The pain felt sharp, like she was having a heart attack. It occurred randomly, and she tolerated it for four days before going to the emergency room because nothing she did relieved it. She had normal EKG and blood tests in the ER, and a normal cardiac workup. The chest pain was worse with eating. She also had difficulty swallowing at the time. The chest pain and swallowing problem got better about three days after she went to the ER, and she has not had any since then. She reports she was going through a really stressful job transition right around the time this happened. She denies abdominal pain, and her bowel movements are normal. 

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Uterine fibroids, anemia

SURGICAL HISTORY
Gallbladder removal several years ago

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for abdominal pain. Normal bowel movements.

PHYSICAL EXAM
General: Looks good.
Abdomen: Mild tenderness to light palpation in the upper abdominal quadrants; about the same on the left and right. Lower belly is not painful or tender to push. Everything else on exam looks normal and good.

ASSESSMENT
Patient is a 52-year-old female with a history of uterine fibroids and anemia, presenting with a past episode of central chest pain, difficulty swallowing, and upper abdominal tenderness that occurred three months ago and has since resolved. ER workup ruled out cardiac causes. Possible etiologies include GERD, dyspepsia, esophagitis, musculoskeletal etiologies, and anxiety. Suspect she had an anxiety attack related to her job transition, plus or minus a contribution from her musculoskeletal etiologies.

PLAN
Discussed options of performing an EGD (upper endoscopy) versus monitoring for symptoms. Given that symptoms occurred three months ago and she has been asymptomatic for so long, likely any esophagitis would already be healed. The patient elected to hold off on the EGD and self-monitor her symptoms. 

INSTRUCTIONS
Call the office if there are any additional episodes of pain, recurrence of symptoms, or any other symptoms of concern, at which point an EGD will be scheduled. Follow up as needed for any other GI complaints.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Renal evaluation for a patient with Smith-Magenis syndrome.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 22-month-old female twin (born at 3 weeks and 3 days) with Smith-Magenis syndrome, diagnosed by a neurologist. She was a twin birth, weighing 4 pounds 8 ounces at birth (her twin was 3 pounds 13 ounces). As an infant, she had feeding issues with stopping breathing while eating, difficulty regulating temperature, and severe reflux (managed by a GI doctor). She was previously managed by a dietician who advised taking her off cow's milk; she currently drinks ripple pea protein milk, water, and sometimes water with a little bit of juice. She drinks well and has around 8 to 10 wet diapers in a 24-hour period. She has developmental delays and did not walk or sit by herself at one year old, but is now crawling and trying to take steps. She is involved in extensive therapies including feeding therapy, occupational therapy, physical therapy, and speech therapy starting soon. She has also seen an orthopedic specialist, an ophthalmologist, an audiologist, and a geneticist. The geneticist informed the family that individuals with this syndrome can have kidney issues, such as fused kidneys, and leg problems. The family lives in Dallas, Georgia, and is here to ensure her kidneys are healthy.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
No acute complaints reported. Drinks well and has approximately 8 to 10 wet diapers per 24 hours.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Smith-Magenis syndrome
Severe reflux

SURGICAL HISTORY
None discussed.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Lives in Dallas, Georgia. Has a 9-year-old brother with autism and a twin sister who is developing typically, running around, and wearing the same size clothes.

FAMILY HISTORY
No family history of kidney failure, dialysis, or transplant.

MEDICATIONS
None listed.

ALLERGIES
None listed.

VITALS
Not explicitly recorded in the transcript.

PHYSICAL EXAM
General: Well-nourished female, slightly fussy when examined.
Head/Eyes: Eyes are small appearing. Ears examined.
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds listened to, normal.
Respiratory: Lungs listened to, normal.
Neuromuscular: Mild hypotonia of the lower extremities and in her arms.
Genitourinary: Normal external female genitalia.

RESULTS
Kidney ultrasound ordered to be completed today.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Katherine is a 22-month-old former 34-week and 3-day twin with Smith-Magenis syndrome, a chromosomal deletion syndrome affecting several organ systems. Congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract have been reported in the literature.
Plan: Obtain a renal ultrasound screening today. If the ultrasound is normal, no further visits with nephrology are needed. If abnormal, follow-up will be scheduled at the Kennesaw (Town Center) location to determine next steps.

INSTRUCTIONS
Complete the ultrasound today downstairs. The nurse will provide paperwork and instructions for the ultrasound. The doctor will call with the results. If results are normal, no further follow-up is necessary; if abnormal, follow-up will be in Kennesaw.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right wrist pain and swelling following a fall.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a female presenting with severe right wrist pain rated at 9 out of 10, accompanied by real swelling, bruising, and a little bit of tingling in the fingers. The injury occurred yesterday morning when she was walking up and down stairs doing laundry, bumped her back against a basket, missed a step while trying to catch a falling basket, and fell onto her outstretched arms. The pain is located along the right wrist and is exacerbated by movement in any direction, including flexion, extension, radial deviation, and adduction/abduction. She notes that keeping the wrist straight and slightly elevated on a pillow at a regular level helps the pain feel better, and ibuprofen helps a little bit. She has tried icing the wrist, applying an ace wrap at home, and taking ibuprofen. She denies any previous injuries to this arm.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for severe pain, swelling, and bruising of the right wrist. No fever.
Neurological: Positive for a little bit of tingling in the fingers; can still feel fingers.
All other systems reviewed and negative unless mentioned.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
None provided in transcript.

SURGICAL HISTORY
None provided in transcript.

SOCIAL HISTORY
None provided in transcript.

FAMILY HISTORY
None provided in transcript.

MEDICATIONS
Ibuprofen (taken for pain)
Ultram 50 mg every six hours (newly prescribed)

ALLERGIES
None provided in transcript.

VITALS
Blood Pressure: 140/70 mmHg
Heart Rate: 80 beats per minute
Temperature: 97.2 degrees Fahrenheit
Respiratory Rate: 20 breaths per minute

PHYSICAL EXAM
General: Head and neck: No adenopathy, no thyromegaly, no carotid bruit.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmur, no rub, no gallop.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Lower Extremities: Palpable pulses, no lower edema.
Upper Extremities: Normal range of movement of shoulders and upper extremities. Right wrist exam: Pain on palpation of both the inside and outside of the wrist. Extreme pain on flexion. Difficulty with extension. Pain on radial deviation and lateral movement. Difficulty making a tight fist. Metacarpals intact. Obvious swelling, ecchymosis, tenderness on palpation, and evidence of potential fracture with palpable bony crepitus.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right wrist: Positive for a Colles' fracture. The fracture appears extra-articular and usually proximal to the radial ulnar joint. Dorsal angulation of the distal fracture fragment is present to a variable degree. Ulnar styloid fracture is present.

ASSESSMENT
Colles' fracture of the right wrist, acute.

PLAN
- Patient will be fitted with a brace for the arm today to be worn for about six weeks.
- Recommended surgical intervention to straighten the wrist and place screws to hold it in place to prevent malformation, to be scheduled as quickly as possible.
- Patient will stay overnight in the hospital for the surgery.
- Prescribed Ultram 50 mg every six hours for pain management.
- Physical therapy to begin a few weeks after surgery, estimated at approximately three times a week to rebuild wrist strength.
- Follow-up checkup in one month to assess healing and determine if a planned vacation in a month can proceed or if it needs to be postponed based on physical therapy status.

INSTRUCTIONS
- Wear the arm brace for about six weeks.
- Keep the wrist straight and slightly elevated (around a regular level, such as when typing) on a pillow for comfort.
- Take Ultram 50 mg every six hours as prescribed for pain.
- Attend scheduled surgery for the right wrist fracture.
- Participate in physical therapy post-surgery as directed.
- Return for a checkup in one month to re-evaluate the wrist and discuss vacation plans.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Abnormal lab work showing low immunoglobulin A level.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a person who was told by their PCP that they had abnormal lab work, specifically a low immunoglobulin A level, which prompted referral. Patient reports feeling anxious about this. PCP ordered the lab work during a recent physical. Patient notes they tend to get colds in the wintertime that linger for a long time, but is unsure if this is more than usual. Denies frequent abdominal infections or diarrhea. Patient denies any family history of immune deficiencies. Patient has a recent diagnosis of type 2 diabetes and was just started on metformin. Denies history of receiving blood transfusions or blood products; attempted to give blood previously but did not qualify due to recent international travel to Zambia.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for frequent diarrhea or abdominal infections. Lingering colds in the wintertime. No other positive or negative symptoms explicitly reported outside of the HPI and physical exam.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Type 2 diabetes mellitus (recently diagnosed).

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient owns a donut shop. History of recent international travel to Zambia.

FAMILY HISTORY
Family is reported to be pretty healthy, with no known immune deficiencies.

MEDICATIONS
Metformin.

ALLERGIES
None mentioned in transcript.

VITALS
Vitals collected by assistants including weight reviewed; no fever and nothing concerning noted.

PHYSICAL EXAM
General: Appears well, no fever.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation, no wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.
Neck: No lymphadenopathy (swollen lymph glands).
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender to palpation, no facial expression of pain.

RESULTS
Review of recent lab work is consistent with an IgA (immunoglobulin A) deficiency.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
IgA deficiency, which is a very common immunodeficiency where one of the body's antibodies is a little lower than normal. Most people live their entire lives without knowing they have it and function normally. Some people may get frequent respiratory tract, sinus, or abdominal infections, but this does not necessarily seem to be the case for this patient. Low likelihood of other co-existing immunodeficiencies, but additional blood work will be ordered to check other antibodies.

INSTRUCTIONS
- Watch for infections that do not stop or are hard to get under control, or changes to the abdominal tract such as severe diarrhea; contact if these occur.
- Get the ordered additional lab work done.
- If needing any blood products between now and the next visit, inform providers of the IgA deficiency due to the risk of a strong reaction.

Flank: Positive CVA tenderness on the right flank, indicating tenderness over the right kidney and potential inflammation.

RESULTS

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Nonhealing right foot ulcer.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a male with a history of diabetes and diabetic neuropathy referred by his primary care physician for a nonhealing right foot ulcer on his right foot. He has been in a boot for about six weeks. He first noticed it after wearing tight shoes, feeling burning and stinging, and finding a blister on the pad of the bottom of his foot around his heel. Recently, he noticed a foul smell, and his dog was smelling his socks. The blister unroofed, revealing thick, soft mushy skin with a bad smell and yellow drainage. 

His primary care doctor started him on antibiotics about 6 days ago (10-day course, currently on day 6 or 7). He reports a temperature of 99.7 checked by his wife, chills requiring an extra blanket, and a cough for the last two days with difficulty catching his breath when walking around the house. He never had nausea or vomiting. The wound initially felt better with antibiotics, but has now turned black around the outside, and he has cramping in his calf muscle. There is a red streak coming up the front of his ankle along the inside portion of his calf muscle, and it is super hot. 

Initially, the wound was stinging, but now it is throbbing like a fire poker in the bottom of his foot. The inside of his calf muscle is really hard, and pushing it causes pain all the way up to his knee behind the kneecap. 

His A1c is normally 6.7 and well-controlled, but over the last two weeks, his blood sugars have been trending in the 300s to 400s, with one spike at 500 to 600. 

The ulcer was caused by a new pair of diabetic shoes after going on a hike to Charlie's Bunion about a week prior to the onset.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Slight fever, chills, no nausea, no vomiting.
Respiratory: Coughing a lot the last two days, difficult time catching breath when walking around the house.
Musculoskeletal: Right foot throbbing pain, calf muscle cramping, hard inside of calf muscle with tenderness radiating up to the knee behind the kneecap.
Neurological: Diabetic neuropathy.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Diabetes mellitus with diabetic neuropathy.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Enjoys hiking with his wife.

MEDICATIONS
Antibiotics prescribed by primary care doctor (day 6 or 7 of a 10-day course).

VITALS
Slight fever noted (99.7 recorded at home).

PHYSICAL EXAM
General: Slight fever recognized. Vitals themselves look good.
Right Foot Exam: Necrotic wound on the heel, approximately 2 x 2 cm. Sloughing of tissue present. Cellulitis and erythema around the area. Foul odor appreciated. No bony exposure. Patient does not feel pressure on the actual affected area of the wound.
Vascular Exam: Bilateral palpable femoral and popliteal pulses present. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses not palpable, but present via Doppler.

RESULTS
Right foot X-ray done today shows no evidence of osteomyelitis (no infection of the bone).

ASSESSMENT
Nonhealing diabetic right foot ulcer with necrotic tissue, sloughing, surrounding cellulitis, erythema, foul odor, and concerning signs including spreading redness and calf swelling/pain. Elevated blood sugars recently trending in the 300s to 400s. No osteomyelitis seen on X-ray.

PLAN
- Order a test to check blood supply for the wound.
- Perform a debridement today in the office.
- Obtain a wound culture.
- Continue current antibiotic therapy (finish the remaining days of the 10-day course initiated by PCP) and determine if additional or changed antibiotic therapy is needed based on the culture results.
- Monitor the condition closely due to the spreading redness, swelling, and calf pain.
- Follow up with endocrinologist to maintain hemoglobin A1c below 7 and closely monitor blood sugars.
- Return for follow-up in seven days.
